lavish

/LAV-ish/ - the stress falls on LAV · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Lavish means given without limits — poured out in abundance; as a verb, to give something without limits.

The publisher's lavish anniversary edition ran to three ribbon bookmarks, gilt page edges, and forty new color plates.

Example

Grandparents who had rationed every nickel of their own youth turned suddenly lavish with the first grandchild — a pony at the birthday, a telescope 'for no reason,' shoes she outgrew before the boxes were recycled.

Lavish describes giving poured past every requirement — not just generous, which credits the spirit of the giver, but overflowing in the visible result: ponies, telescopes, boxes upon boxes of shoes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

extravagant: Extravagant means spending or giving beyond what sense allows — the word arrives with a raised eyebrow. Lavish shares the abundance but not the frown: lavish admires the overflowing hand, extravagant audits it.

unstinting: Unstinting means holding nothing back — giving without stint or limit, usually said of effort, praise, or support. It measures the giver's steadiness; lavish measures the poured-out result you can see on the table.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

meager: thin, scanty, barely enough to go around

grudging: given reluctantly, in the smallest amount duty allows

Where it sits · how freely the giving pours

generous → lavish → extravagant

generous vs. lavish: Generous is milder than lavish: a generous host gives gladly and amply, while a lavish one pours it out past all keeping track — more courses, more gifts, more everything.

extravagant vs. lavish: Extravagant goes further than lavish — lavish giving still earns admiring gasps, but extravagant spending has crossed into excess that even the admirers call unwise.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — lav: to wash, to pour (Latin lavare)

Suffix — -ish: adjective ending (reshaped in English from French -asse)

Put it together: Latin lavare, 'to wash,' flowed into Old French lavasse — a drenching downpour of rain. English borrowed the downpour and kept the image: what is lavish comes down like that rain, poured out without measure.

Use the root in a new word: deluge: 'Deluge,' the crossword clue said — six letters — and Dad refused every offer of help until he had gotten it himself.

Root Check

Word Choice

admiring / warm

Lavish admires abundance: praise, gifts, or spending poured out past what anyone required, described with a smile. Extravagant covers the same overflow with a frown — spending past sense — and generous credits the giver's spirit rather than the size of what lands on the table. As a verb, lavish takes 'on': grandparents lavish attention on the baby.
